solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Schoolgirl assuming goofball leaving college fails

indicators.note: to assume is to take on or take in, so one word takes another inside itself

parts.note: a schoolgirl is addressed as Miss

indicators.note: something leaving goes away, so a letter departs from the word it was part of

parts.note: a dumb cluck is a stupid person
C is the abbreviation for college

explanation.surface: A schoolgirl who acts the fool and drops out of college ends up failing.
explanation.walkthrough: A dumb cluck is American slang for a fool. 'Fails' is the definition, a verb, and misluck is an old word found in Chambers.
explanation.definitionFit: To misluck is an old word meaning to meet with bad luck or come to grief, so someone who mislucks does not succeed.

clue.text: Periodic series of visits given by artist Gustav cut short?

indicators.note: cut short means the painter's surname loses its last letter before being read backwards

parts.note: Gustav Klimt is the Austrian painter whose surname supplies the letters

explanation.surface: The painter Gustav Klimt is credited with a series of regular visits that ended early.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: take the solution's first word, turn it as its second word says, and KLIM appears, which is KLIMT cut short.
explanation.definitionFit: A milkman's daily delivery route, and by extension any routine series of calls, is a periodic series of visits.

clue.text: One nil again it's tight, conveying character of Napoli?

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: tight means drunk, and drunken letters reel into a different order

parts.note: eleven letters taken as written, ready to be mixed

explanation.surface: A football report: one-nil again, a tight game, very much in the style of Napoli.
explanation.walkthrough: The football scoreline and 'tight' as a close game are pure surface; 'tight' is the drunk anagram signal and 'one' is simply I placed in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Italianising means giving something an Italian flavour, and Napoli is the Italian name for Naples, so the city's character is Italian.

clue.text: Teachers adopting rule to punish

indicators.note: to adopt is to take in, so one word takes a letter inside itself

parts.note: the teaching staff of a school
R is the abbreviation for rule

explanation.surface: Teachers bring in a new rule in order to discipline pupils.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes inside STAFF. Straff is a variant spelling of strafe, which can mean to punish or reprimand severely.
explanation.definitionFit: Strafe, spelt straff in Chambers too, means to bombard or attack, and by extension to chastise someone harshly.

clue.text: Heading off from dull Scottish match that's slow

indicators.note: a heading is the top, so taking it off drops the first letter

parts.note: a dull blade is blunt

explanation.surface: A dreary, slow-moving football match in Scotland, with the headers taken out of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Match' looks like a sporting fixture, but it is the kind you strike: a slow match is a slow-burning fuse used to fire old guns.
explanation.definitionFit: Lunt is a Scots word for a slow match, the smouldering cord used to light gunpowder or cannon.

clue.text: With end of race emerging instructs rowers perhaps to be fastening

indicators.note: something emerging comes out, so a letter comes out of the word around it

parts.note: to coach is to instruct

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of race
rowers form a crew, among other examples

explanation.surface: At the finish of a boat race, someone coaches the rowing eight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rowers perhaps' signals an example: rowers make up one kind of team. 'Fastening' is a noun here, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A coach screw is a large square-headed wood screw, a kind of fastener used in heavy timber work.

clue.text: Scottish court's to stay and be in session around Sabbath

indicators.note: around places one word on either side of another

parts.note: a court sits when it is in session
S is the abbreviation for Sabbath

explanation.surface: A Scottish court must pause, yet also sit on the Sabbath.
explanation.walkthrough: S goes inside SIT. Sist is a term of Scots law; the definition is the whole phrase saying what a Scottish court does.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots law, to sist is to stay or suspend proceedings, the equivalent of an English court granting a stay.

clue.text: Siri — personal assistant (first seen in Apple Newton?)

parts.note: PA is the usual abbreviation for personal assistant

indicators.note: what is seen first in each word is its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Siri, Apple's voice assistant, as a successor to the old Apple Newton handheld.
explanation.walkthrough: Siri looks like Apple's software, and Apple Newton like the 1990s gadget, but siri is also a word for betel, and that is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Paan is betel leaf wrapped round areca nut and spices for chewing; siri is another name for the betel it is made from.

clue.text: A once vast landmass, supposedly crowded area by river

indicators.note: by means next to, so one piece sits beside the next

parts.note: pang is a Scots adjective meaning crammed full
A is the abbreviation for area
ea is an old word for a river

explanation.surface: A crowded spot beside a river, imagined as a vast landmass long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supposedly' belongs with the definition: the single ancient supercontinent is a reconstruction by geologists, not something anyone saw.
explanation.definitionFit: Pangaea is the supercontinent that geologists believe joined all of Earth's land before it split apart some 200 million years ago.

clue.text: What you might get up with largely in the morning?

definitions.text: What you might get up with largely in the morning?

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another

parts.note: AM is the abbreviation for the morning
the word large without its last two letters

explanation.surface: A gentle question about what usually gets you out of bed in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: most of LARGE sits inside AM.
explanation.definitionFit: An alarm clock is the device most people wake to, so it is what you might get up with each day.

clue.text: French suddenly to get better after a lecturer inspires one stumped

indicators.note: after places one piece behind the other

parts.note: taken as written
L is the abbreviation for lecturer

indicators.note: to inspire is literally to breathe in, so one word draws others inside it

parts.note: to get better is to improve
the Roman numeral for one
st is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for stumped

explanation.surface: A French speaker is suddenly cured after a lecture that leaves one baffled.
explanation.walkthrough: Stumped is a cricket dismissal, written st on scorecards, not bafflement. 'French suddenly' tells you the answer is a French phrase meaning suddenly.
explanation.definitionFit: À l'improviste is a French expression meaning unexpectedly or without warning, which is what suddenly conveys.

clue.text: DJ less tense with words admitting I like a wife

indicators.note: less means without, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: a DJ is a dinner jacket, a tux in American English
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so one word takes a letter inside

parts.note: done with spoken words rather than in writing
taken as written

explanation.surface: A disc jockey, calmer now, chats on air about being rather wifely.
explanation.walkthrough: DJ is not a disc jockey here but a dinner jacket, which Americans call a tux. 'Less tense' looks like calmer, but it removes T.
explanation.definitionFit: Uxorial comes from Latin uxor, a spouse who is female, so uxorially describes behaving in the manner of one.

clue.text: In some places discovers networks hosting user's terminal

indicators.note: a host has a guest within, so one word holds a letter inside

parts.note: LANs are local area networks

indicators.note: a terminal is an end point, so only the final letter is used

parts.note: the last letter of user

explanation.surface: Someone finds computer networks in various places that serve a user's terminal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terminal' looks like a computer screen in this surface, but it picks the end letter. 'In some places' marks a dialect word.
explanation.definitionFit: Larn is a dialect form of learn, and to learn something can mean to find it out, so larns means finds out.

clue.text: Duck to protect beanpole

parts.note: to shield is to protect
a beanpole is a thin person, and so is a rake

explanation.surface: Someone ducks down to protect a tall stick in the vegetable garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Duck' reads as a verb, to dodge, but it is the bird. Rake and beanpole are both words for a very thin, tall person.
explanation.definitionFit: Shieldrake is an old spelling of sheldrake, the male shelduck, a large pied waterbird.

clue.text: Medic's name in project

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

parts.note: to sail can mean to jut out or project
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A doctor's name appears in a research project.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Medic' looks like a doctor, but medick is also a clover-like plant; one kind with coiled pods is called the snail.
explanation.definitionFit: Snail is a name for the snail medick, a plant of the pea family whose spiral seed pods resemble snail shells.

clue.text: Gossip going round school coffee morning?

indicators.note: something going round turns back on itself, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: gossip is idle talk
SCH is the abbreviation for school

explanation.surface: Gossip spreading around the school gate at a parents' coffee morning.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark admits that a klatsch need not be in the morning: the word is German for gossip, borrowed as in coffee klatsch.
explanation.definitionFit: A klatsch is an informal social gathering for coffee and chat, which is what a coffee morning is.

clue.text: Serb perhaps turns to embrace close Christian community

indicators.note: an embrace wraps arms around, so one word encloses another
a word that turns faces the other way, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: a Serb is one example of a Slav
close, as in closely packed, means dense

explanation.surface: A Serb in turn grows fond of a close-knit Christian group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Serb perhaps' gives an example of a wider group, the Slavs. 'Close' is the adjective meaning tightly packed, not the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The Valdenses, better known as the Waldenses, were a medieval Christian movement founded by Peter Waldo, later a Protestant church.

clue.text: Raging pains once leaving one of Canaries

indicators.note: something leaving departs, so those letters are taken away

parts.note: Tenerife is the largest of the Canary Islands
tene is an archaic word for grief or sorrow

explanation.surface: Sorrow and suffering of old fade as someone leaves Tenerife for home.
explanation.walkthrough: TENE comes off the front of TENERIFE. 'Raging' is used as of a disease that is spreading.
explanation.definitionFit: A disease that is raging is widespread and out of control, and rife means prevalent in just that way.

clue.text: A redcap spotted in friend's floating garden

indicators.note: something spotted in a place is found inside it

parts.note: china means mate, from Cockney rhyming slang china plate
taken as written
a redcap is a British military policeman, an MP

explanation.surface: A military policeman is seen in a friend's water garden.
explanation.walkthrough: Redcap is British slang for a military policeman, from their red caps; china is Cockney rhyming slang for a mate, from china plate.
explanation.definitionFit: A chinampa is an artificial island used for farming in the shallow lakes of Mexico, often called a floating garden.

clue.text: Imitation gem that could be paler?

definitions.meaning: surface reading: a fake jewel, perhaps one paler than the real thing
setter's reading: a reverse clue, where the answer read as an anagram instruction turns the gem's name into paler

explanation.surface: A cheap fake jewel that might look a bit washed out.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as wordplay: 'false' is an anagram signal and the gem's name, rearranged, spells paler. The question mark warns of the reversed trick.
explanation.definitionFit: A false pearl is an imitation of a real one, made of glass or plastic coated to look lustrous.

clue.text: I start to climb in lopped fruit trees

indicators.note: in places I and the first letter inside the other letters
lopped means the head is cut off the fruit

parts.note: mangos are tropical fruit

indicators.note: start to gives the opening letter of climb

explanation.surface: Someone begins climbing among pruned fruit trees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lopped' takes M from MANGOS to leave ANGOS, with I and C inserted.
explanation.definitionFit: The angico is a South American leguminous tree yielding gum and timber; the plural names several.

clue.text: Doubtful about uni complex having one centre?

indicators.note: about means around, so one word goes round another

parts.note: something doubtful is unclear

indicators.note: complex means intricate or tangled, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is unsure about a university campus centred on a single hub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uni complex' looks like a campus, but 'complex' only mixes the three letters before them, which then sit inside UNCLEAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Uninuclear is a biology term for a cell with a single nucleus, and a nucleus is the cell's central body.

clue.text: Show succeeded being very secure again

indicators.note: succeeded being very means the letter for succeeded stands where the letter for very was

parts.note: to show is to reveal
S is the abbreviation for succeeded, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: A show was a hit, being very secure in its run once more.
explanation.walkthrough: Start with REVEAL (show); 'succeeded being very' asks for S to take the place of V, giving RESEAL.
explanation.definitionFit: To reseal something is to close or fasten it up again, making it secure once more.

clue.text: Some vendors dragging back skinflints

indicators.note: going back means running in the opposite direction
some means only part, so the letters are a portion of the words that follow

parts.note: the tail of the first word and most of the second

explanation.surface: Some market traders drag their feet, the stingy lot.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run backwards across the join of the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: A niggard is a miserly person who begrudges spending, the same meaning as a skinflint.

clue.text: Gin blended with case of exquisite spirit

indicators.note: a blend mixes things together, so these letters are stirred into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outer shell, its first and last letters

parts.note: the first and last letters of exquisite

explanation.surface: Gin mixed into a cocktail gives an excellent spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirit' looks like alcohol to go with the gin, but it is a supernatural being.
explanation.definitionFit: A genie is a spirit of Arabian folklore, like the one bound to Aladdin's lamp.

clue.text: Old dear's certainly not thick skinned

definitions.note: dear here is the adjective, beloved or precious

indicators.note: skinned means the outer layer is peeled away, so the first and last letters go

parts.note: someone certainly not thick, that is not stupid, is clever

explanation.surface: Someone protests that an elderly lady is quite sensitive, not thick-skinned at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old dear' looks like an affectionate name for an elderly woman, but it means 'dear' in an old sense; the 's is 'is'. Skinning CLEVER removes its C and R.
explanation.definitionFit: Leve is an archaic spelling of lief, an obsolete adjective meaning beloved or precious.

clue.text: Restrict essential ingredient of fasting diet

parts.note: to ban is to restrict

indicators.note: the essential part of a word is its heart, the middle letter

parts.note: the middle letter of fasting

explanation.surface: Cutting back is the key to any fasting regime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diet' here is a verb. Bant comes from William Banting, a Victorian who popularised a low-carbohydrate slimming plan.
explanation.definitionFit: To bant is to follow Banting's slimming regime, so it means to go on a diet to lose weight.

clue.text: Enzyme burst ripens last of produce

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter

parts.note: the final letter of produce

indicators.note: something burst flies apart, so the letters scatter into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A burst of enzyme activity ripens the last of the harvest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Burst' looks like a verb about the enzyme, but it is the anagram signal on the six letters after it, plus one more.
explanation.definitionFit: Erepsin is a mixture of digestive proteins secreted in the small intestine that breaks peptides down into amino acids.

clue.text: Atlantic cod once found round bottom of ocean

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so one word goes on both sides of a letter

parts.note: cod was an old word for a pod or husk, as in peascod

indicators.note: in a down answer the bottom of a word is its last letter

parts.note: the final letter of ocean

explanation.surface: An Atlantic cod of olden times was found near the ocean floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Atlantic cod' reads as the fish, but 'Atlantic' alone defines and 'cod once' is an archaic word. 'Bottom of' picks the last letter of ocean.
explanation.definitionFit: The pond is a jocular name for the Atlantic Ocean, as in 'across the pond' between Britain and America.

clue.text: Jagger perhaps wanting a fabric for embroidery

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so a letter is missing

parts.note: Bianca Jagger, the former wife of Mick Jagger
taken as written

explanation.surface: Mick Jagger, perhaps, wants some fabric for a bit of needlework.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jagger' points to Mick, but the Jagger needed is Bianca; one of her A's goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Binca is an open, evenly woven cotton cloth with clear holes, used especially by children learning cross-stitch.

clue.text: Club loses deposit

indicators.note: to club is to beat, and beaten letters are knocked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A football club loses its deposit, perhaps on a ground or a transfer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club' looks like the subject of the sentence, but it is a verb meaning beat, signalling the rearrangement; 'deposit' is geological.
explanation.definitionFit: Loess is a fine yellowish silt laid down by wind, a sediment that geologists call a deposit.

clue.text: Thin paper's a failure checking first of images, flipping ink's running

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over end to end
to check is to hold back, so one word holds a letter in its grip

parts.note: a no-no is a failure or non-starter

indicators.note: the first of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of images

indicators.note: running colours smear and spread, so the letters lose their order

parts.note: taken as written, with the S

explanation.surface: A thin paper is useless at holding pictures, the ink smudging everywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: A no-no is something not allowed, and Chambers also gives it as a failure or non-starter. 'Flipping' looks like a mild British curse, but it turns the first assembled piece round.
explanation.definitionFit: Onionskin is a very thin, translucent, glazed paper, named for its likeness to the papery layers of an onion.

clue.text: Week off carries on a long time

indicators.note: off means removed, so that letter is taken away

parts.note: to carry on a war is to wage it
W is the abbreviation for week

explanation.surface: A week off work drags on for what seems forever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Week off' looks like a holiday, but it means W is removed from the following word.
explanation.definitionFit: Ages is an informal plural meaning a very long period, as in 'I waited for ages'.

clue.text: Pipes pretty rarely redirected

parts.note: twee is sweetly pretty, often overly so

indicators.note: redirected means sent the other way, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: seld is an archaic word for seldom

explanation.surface: Plumbing pipes are seldom rerouted for the sake of looking nice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pipes' reads as tubes, but it is a verb: to play a pipe. Twee is British for affectedly pretty.
explanation.definitionFit: To tweedle is to play casually on a pipe or fiddle, so tweedles means pipes in the musical sense.
